activities.caption: file each bar by its cooling route
activities.name: wmbForgeBuckets

config.prompt: One bar cooled slowly on the bench, one plunged into water — file each observation:

items.label: bends in your hands and stays bent
hard enough to scratch mineral, brittle enough to snap
iron atoms trapped in a hard, strained lattice
iron atoms settled into soft, orderly layers

config.why: Identical atoms — iron with a trace of carbon — and only the cooling route differs. The route sets the arrangement, and the arrangement sets the behaviour.

config.prompt: The causal spine, in working order — drag the links into place:
items: Processing: quench the blade or cool it slowly
Structure: strained martensite lattice, or orderly pearlite layers
Properties: hard and brittle, or soft and ductile
Performance: an edge that holds, or a spring that forgives
config.why: How you make a thing sets the arrangement of its atoms; the arrangement sets the properties; the properties set what the thing can do.

activities.anchor: firing alpha particles at gold foil
activities.caption: the atom-model chronology, scrubbable
activities.name: wmbAtomTimeline

events.title: Dalton's spheres
events.text: Indivisible atoms with fixed masses, proposed to explain whole-number combining ratios.

events.title: Thomson's electron
events.text: A particle far lighter than any atom; the plum-pudding atom follows.

events.title: Rutherford's nucleus
events.text: A tiny fraction of the shot returns: nearly all mass and positive charge sit in a nucleus 100,000× smaller than the atom.

events.title: Bohr's orbits
events.text: Electrons occupy only certain allowed orbits.

events.title: Quantum orbitals
events.text: Schrödinger and others replace orbits with probability clouds.

activities.anchor: barcode readable from a metre away
activities.caption: pair each line-spectrum readout with what makes it work
activities.name: wmbSpectrumMatch

config.prompt: One phenomenon, four readouts — pair each use with the fact that powers it:

pairs.left: a new element found in the Sun (1868)
pairs.right: an unmatched yellow line, 27 years before the element turned up on Earth
that gas's own emission pattern — its spectrum
each element's pattern is unique, so a sample's light names it
the pattern travels in the starlight itself

config.why: The lines are fixed because the energy levels are fixed — and each element's pattern is unique.

activities.caption: one line of the reading note is wrong
activities.name: wmbMapSpot

config.prompt: A student's note on the periodic table — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: The table is sorted by outer-electron count, which repeats down the columns.
Lithium, sodium and potassium share a column, so all are soft, reactive metals.
Sodium and chlorine are neighbours in a row, so the two behave almost alike.
In reality one is a violent metal, the other a poisonous reactive gas.
Read the table vertically for behaviour, horizontally for the shift from metal to non-metal.
config.correction: Row-neighbours can be opposites: the sorting matches outer-electron counts down columns, so sodium's true near-twin is potassium — same column, next row.
config.why: Along a row the behaviour shifts steadily from metallic to non-metallic, so adjacent elements can sit at opposite extremes.

activities.anchor: the discipline's thesis in one comparison
activities.caption: drag the divider — two structures, a single element
activities.name: wmbCarbonCompare

config.prompt: Two structures of a single element — drag to see what each arrangement buys:

before.label: every atom bonded to four neighbours
before.text: A rigid 3D tetrahedral network: the hardest natural material, a superb abrasive, an electrical insulator.

after.label: each atom bonded to only three
after.text: Flat sheets held to each other by feeble forces: soft enough to write with, slippery enough to lubricate.

config.why: Same element, different structure, opposite properties — arrangement, not composition, decides behaviour.

activities.anchor: draw the line of constant performance
activities.caption: call the material index
activities.name: wmbAshbyEstimate

config.prompt: Steel's light-stiff index (E ÷ ρ) is about 26 GPa per (t/m³). Carbon-fibre composites reach roughly four times that. What figure do they hit?
config.why: About 104 — four times steel's 26 — which is the whole aviation and Formula 1 material story in a single number.
config.context: A light, stiff tie-rod maximises E ÷ ρ; a light, stiff panel wants ∛E ÷ ρ instead, and the geometry can change the winner.

activities.caption: true or false — slope, height, area
activities.name: wmbTripleJudge

statements.s: Strong and stiff mean the same thing in materials science.
statements.why: Strength is the stress carried before yielding (the height); stiffness is the stretch per unit load (the slope) — two different readings of one curve.

statements.s: Nothing about a sample's shape, size or heat treatment changes Young's modulus — it comes from the bonds.
statements.why: The elastic slope is a direct readout of bonding strength.

statements.s: A floppy material cannot be tough.
statements.why: Rubber is floppy and remarkably tough — stiffness and toughness are separate dials.

statements.s: Glass must be softer than aluminium because it fails far more easily.
statements.why: Glass is about as stiff as aluminium (E ≈ 70 GPa); it fails without warning because it is brittle, not because it is soft.
